production_notes: [VERSION] Google Slides steps (Insert > Chart > From Sheets, linking and updating charts, speaker notes) and Looker Studio chart download or export options must be checked against the live tools before recording. The narration mentions linking a chart from Sheets and using a screenshot from Looker Studio only; it does not name menu paths or download options.
Judgement call (from the curriculum): this lesson uses Google Slides or a similar free tool, which is not in the brief's tools_free_first; charts come from Google Sheets or Looker Studio.

Elena, the Bucharest bakery client and all figures are fictional. Spoken numbers match content.md: weekend revenue 5,000 to 5,900 lei = 18% (900 ÷ 5,000); Saturday 3,300 of 5,900 = about 56%, not 60%; six months of data. The hook's 31% vs 13% is the hypothetical meeting question from content.md.
Last lesson of the course: the CTA congratulates learners and points to the capstone submission (report + findings log, checklist and rubric on the course page).

Hook.voiceover: Your slides look professional, the charts are clear, and the story makes sense. Then someone in the meeting asks, the chart says thirty-one percent, but the title says thirteen percent. Which is right? One wrong number can make people doubt everything else you show.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you planned five messages. Now you turn them into slides, in Google Slides or a similar free tool.

slide.title: Building and Reviewing Your Five-Slide Report
slide.body: AI-Powered Data Analysis (No Code) · Lesson 14 of 14 · Capstone step 3

Explain.voiceover: Here are the five slides. Slide one is the question. The business question, the dataset with its source, period and number of rows, and one sentence on how you analysed it. Slide two is the key finding. The main message as the title, and one large number that supports it. Slide three is the evidence. One to three charts, each with a title that states its finding.

slide.title: The five slides
slide.body: 1. The question: business question, dataset (source, period, rows), method in one sentence · 2. The key finding: message as title + one large number · 3. The evidence: 1–3 charts with finding titles · 4. and 5. dimmed

Explain.voiceover: Slide four is the recommendation. A specific action, who should do it, and how to measure whether it worked. Slide five is the limits. What the data cannot show, such as a small sample, missing columns, correlation rather than cause, or data from one period only.

slide.title: The five slides
slide.body: 4. The recommendation: action · who · how to measure · 5. The limits: small sample · missing columns · correlation, not cause · one period only

Explain.voiceover: For the charts, you can insert a chart from Google Sheets and link it to the spreadsheet, so it can be updated if the data changes. From Looker Studio, you can use a screenshot of a chart. Keep one message per slide, large text and few words. Put extra detail in the speaker notes.

slide.title: Adding charts
slide.body: Google Sheets chart → linked chart on slide (update icon) · Looker Studio chart → screenshot on slide. Slide mock-up: one message, large text; speaker notes panel below with extra detail.

Explain.voiceover: AI can help with wording. Paste your five messages and ask for shorter titles, or ask what a manager might question. But do not paste raw personal or confidential data to do this.

slide.title: AI for wording
slide.body: Paste your five messages → shorter titles · 'What might a manager question?' · Never paste raw personal or confidential data

Explain.voiceover: Then comes the final check. Before you share the report, check every number on every slide against your source data. Make a small check table with four columns. The slide, the number shown, where it comes from, and match or fix. Check chart titles, labels and speaker notes too.

slide.title: The number check table
slide.body: Table header: Slide | Number shown | Source (pivot table cell or formula) | Match or fix. Icons: titles · labels · speaker notes

Explain.voiceover: Numbers change when you round them, copy them or rewrite a title. So this check comes last.
It is like a pilot's checklist before take-off. The pilot has flown many times and knows the aircraft well. But the pilot still checks every item, because one missed item can cause serious problems.
Explain.stock_query: pilot going through checklist in cockpit

Demonstrate.voiceover: Elena is a small business consultant in Bucharest, Romania. She has built a five-slide report for a fictional bakery client, about weekend sales.
Demonstrate.stock_query: consultant showing slides to bakery owner

Demonstrate.voiceover: She makes her check table. Slide two says weekend sales grew eighteen percent. Her pivot table shows weekend revenue rising from five thousand to five thousand nine hundred lei. Nine hundred divided by five thousand is eighteen percent. Match.

slide.title: Check table: slide 2
slide.body: Slide 2: 'Weekend sales grew 18%' | Pivot table: 5,000 → 5,900 lei; (5,900 − 5,000) ÷ 5,000 = 18% → Match ✓

Demonstrate.voiceover: Slide three's chart title says Saturday is sixty percent of weekend sales. But the pivot table shows three thousand three hundred of five thousand nine hundred, which is about fifty-six percent. The AI had suggested the title from an earlier version of the data.

slide.title: Check table: slide 3
slide.body: Slide 3 title: 'Saturday is 60% of weekend sales' | Pivot table: 3,300 of 5,900 = about 56% → Fix (amber)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Fix. She changes the title to, Saturday brings in more than half of weekend sales, fifty-six percent.

slide.title: Corrected title
slide.body: 'Saturday brings in more than half of weekend sales (56%)'

Demonstrate.voiceover: On slide five, she writes the limits. The data covers only six months, and a new competitor opened nearby during that time, which may affect the results. In the speaker notes, she adds how she cleaned the data, and how many rows she used.

slide.title: Elena's limits slide
slide.body: Only six months of data · A new competitor opened nearby during that time · Speaker notes: how the data was cleaned and how many rows were used

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to check the numbers once, early, and then keep editing titles and charts. Each edit is a new chance for an error. Another is to hide the limits. A clear limits slide makes the report more trustworthy, not less.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the five slides are the question, the key finding, the evidence, the recommendation, and the limits of the analysis. Second, insert charts from Google Sheets or Looker Studio, keep one message per slide, and put detail in the speaker notes. Third, as the very last step, check every number on every slide against the source data, with a check table.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Question · key finding · evidence · recommendation · limits. 2. Charts from Sheets or Looker Studio; one message per slide; detail in notes. 3. Last step: check every number.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. This is capstone step three. Build your five-slide insight report, check every number against your data, and add a speaker note that explains the limits of your analysis. Then submit your report with your findings log, using the checklist and rubric on the course page.

slide.title: Submit your capstone
slide.body: Five-slide insight report · check table: every number 'match' · speaker note on limits · findings log · checklist and rubric on the course page

CTA.voiceover: Congratulations on finishing AI-Powered Data Analysis. You can now clean, analyse, chart and explain data with AI, and check every number before you share it. Well done, and good luck with your report.
